# X-TURING: Towards an Enhanced and Efficient Turing Test for Long-Term Dialogue Agents

Weiqi Wu, Hongqiu Wu, Hai Zhao†

$^{1}$ School of Computer Science, Shanghai Jiao Tong University

$^{2}$ Key Laboratory of Shanghai Education Commission for Intelligent Interaction and Cognitive Engineering, Shanghai Jiao Tong University

$^{3}$ Shanghai Key Laboratory of Trusted Data Circulation and Governance in Web3

{wuwq1022,wuhongqiu}@sjtu.edu.cn,

zhaohai@cs.sjtu.edu.cn

# Abstract

The Turing test examines whether AIs exhibit human-like behaviour in natural language conversations. The traditional setting limits each participant to one message at a time and requires constant human participation. This fails to reflect a natural conversational style and hinders the evaluation of dialogue agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex and prolonged interactions. This paper proposes X-TURING, which enhances the original test with a burst dialogue pattern, allowing more dynamic exchanges using consecutive messages. It further reduces human workload by iteratively generating dialogues that simulate the long-term interaction between the agent and a human to compose the majority of the test process. With the pseudo-dialogue history, the agent then engages in a shorter dialogue with a real human, which is paired with a human-human conversation on the same topic to be judged using questionnaires. We introduce the $X$ -Turn Pass-Rate metric to assess the human likeness of LLMs across varying durations. While LLMs like GPT-4 initially perform well, achieving pass rates of $51.9\%$ and $38.9\%$ during 3 turns and 10 turns of dialogues respectively, their performance drops as the dialogue progresses, which underscores the difficulty in maintaining consistency in the long term. $^{\ddagger}$

# 1 Introduction

The Turing Test, originally called the imitation game by Alan Turing in 1950, is a test of whether a machine can behave indistinguishably from a human (Turing, 1950). During the test, a human integrator converses in natural language with both a human and an AI, then tries to identify which is

which. The AI is considered to pass the test if it can convincingly mimic human responses so that the integrator misidentifies it as a human participant. Contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs) (OpenAI, 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023; Anthropic, 2024) demonstrate remarkable language generation capabilities in various scenarios (Wu et al., 2024a). These advancements have sparked increasing interest in whether the latest LLMs can pass the Turing test (Jones and Bergen, 2024).

However, the traditional Turing test has several limitations: (1) The dialogue follows a strict ping-pong structure, unlike natural communication where people may send multiple messages in a row to convey a statement. (2) The need for continuous human involvement in interactions with the test subject limits test duration to under ten min

s several limitations: (1) The dialogue follows a strict ping-pong structure, unlike natural communication where people may send multiple messages in a row to convey a statement. (2) The need for continuous human involvement in interactions with the test subject limits test duration to under ten minutes, leaving long-term evaluation unexplored. (3) Measuring test duration in minutes ignores individual differences in reading, thinking, and typing speeds, potentially disadvantageing some participants.

To address these issues, we propose X-TURING, a new framework designed to conduct an efficient Turing test for LLM-based dialogue agents with an enhanced dialogue pattern that aligns with daily communication among humans. Firstly, we break the constraint of a single message each turn to allow users to send multiple messages in rapid succession without waiting for a response. As illustrated in Figure 1, this dynamic exchange mirrors natural text-based human interactions and challenges LLMs to maintain coherence and relevance in more diverse interactions. We construct chatbots for the test by prompting LLMs with social platform dialogue records from a real-life human.

Given the exhausting nature of long-term Turing test, we propose enhancing its efficiency by approximating real human-machine interactions through dialogue generation techniques (Soudani et al., 2024), and using questionnaires instead of

According to psychological research on the serial position effect (Murdock and Bennet, 1962), the first and last parts of a sequence are likely to be most memorable and thus critical for judgment. As it is more challenging for LLMs to maintain consistency and coherence over long-term interactions (Park et al., 2023; Bubeck et al., 2023), our evaluation focuses on the last few turns of the conversation. Therefore, we propose pseudo-dialogue generation to allow the model to direct this progression on its own. It involves iteratively generating multi-turn dialogues to reflect the LLM's evolving performance over time. Human participants only need to converse subsequently for a few more turns, as depicted in Figure 1. By focusing the evaluation on the final interaction turns, we can provide a comprehensive assessment while significantly reducing the human workload, effectively making the Turing test scalable in terms of interaction length.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- We extend the classical Turing test with burst dialogue, more closely reflecting natural human communication.

# 2 Related Work

Turing Test Turing test and its variations have been extensively applied to assess AI across multiple domains, including dialogue interaction (Jones and Bergen, 2024; Lowe et al., 2017), question answering(Ng et al., 2024), text generation (Helm et al., 2023; Uchendu et al., 2021), and visual tasks (Imanpour et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). These evaluations, which involve distinguishing between human-generated and AI-generated content (Gao and Emami, 2023) or inferring from solely the content (Jannai et al., 2023), serve as essential benchmarks for AI models. Existing works proposing the limitations of Turing tests focus on whether passing the test indicates intelligence accurately (Freitas et al., 2020) or comprehensively (Lee et al., 2023). We rather focus on its feasibility issue in long-term evaluation and enhance the flexibility of the communication pattern.

Role-play with LLMs A common tactic in Turing tests is to assign LLMs the role of a specific

human character (Jannai et al., 2023), leveraging their proficiency in adopting varied attributes and conversational styles (Wu et al., 2024b; Shanahan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a). Prompting the model with character profiles (Li et al., 2023; Tao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023b; Chen et al., 2023c) or key utterances (Han et al., 2022; Boyd et al., 2020) proves to be a more efficient method, compared with fine-tuning on massive character data (Shao et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2024). By utilizing the dialogue history of the designated individual, we can develop a role-playing chatbot that effectively handles various dialogue forms and scenarios.

Dialogue Generation The development of synthetic dialogue data has provided a more efficient and scalable approach to data creation and augmentation (Soudani et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2017). Advancements in dialogue generation have been facilitated by LLMs (Abdullin et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023b,a; Kim et al., 2022a; Abbasiantaeb et al., 2023), which excel at creating contextually relevant and diverse conversations by prompted turn-by-turn (Lee et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022b) or even in just one go (Jandaghi et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a). By iteratively generating dialogues

# 3 X-TURING

# 3.1 Burst Dialogue v.s. Ping-pong Dialogue

Conversations with a ping-pong structure are considered the standard form of human-machine interaction and are commonly used in the Turing Test, where each user message is followed by a system response to form a strict back-and-forth pattern. However, in real life, people usually send multiple messages in rapid succession without waiting for the other's response and the response can also consist of multiple messages. We define this communication pattern as Burst Dialogue and delve into the performance of LLMs in this setting.

In a ping-pong dialogue, a turn is naturally formed by pairing each user message with the corresponding system response. In contrast, burst dialogue involves a more flexible information exchange, where interruption and continuation can happen frequently for both sides. For simplicity, a turn of burst dialogue is defined as a consecutive

![](images/a460a9cadac4e4c73c68b39f19542d98b597d24436d4dd40d4bc60df67905952.jpg)  
Figure 2: Chatbot system enabling burst dialogue.

series of user messages followed by the system's responses before the next user message. Despite potential unbalanced exchange, burst dialogue is more dynamic and aligns more closely with the natural human communication pattern. It challenges the model to handle overlapping and rapidly evolving conversational contexts, thereby testing its ability to maintain coherence and relevance in real-time interactions. Hence, we extend the classical ping-pong dialogue setting to assess how well LLMs manage more realistic conversational dynamics.

# 3.2 Chatbot Construction

The Turing test necessitates the deployment of a chatbot to judge its text-based conversation ability. Instead of manually crafting detailed profiles for individuals, we construct the dialogue agent based on real-life dialogue history, which provides essential clues for generating responses that emulate the target personality, linguistic style and content. To achieve this, we gather multi-turn text-based social platform chat records for each target individual, which are burst conversational data consisting of timestamps and message content. The LLM is then instructed to maintain consistency with the conversation style with the prompt presented in Appendix B.1. For ping-pong dialogues, we retain only the first message of a consecutive series from the same person and manually filter out meaningless turns.

To implement a burst messaging chatbot, we employ three modules working synchronously as shown in Figure 2: $\bullet$ Input Listener: to collect

user messages; $\bullet$ Model Caller: to query the LLM to generate responses; $\bullet$ Output Sender: to manage the delivery of system responses based on the timestamps. The system introduces a brief time interval $\hat{t}$ before processing the first batch of user inputs to allow the user to fully express themselves. After $\hat{t}$ , the Input Listener processes all user messages collectively for the Model Caller to generate a response.

Following the given burst dialogue data and the instruction, the chatbot generates consecutive messages in a response that can be sent to the user and added to the dialogue history by the Output Sender based on their respective timestamps. In case of any timestamp errors, e.g., being earlier than the current timestamp, we resample the message sending time. A message consisting of $n$ characters is sent after a delay $d$ of around 0.3s per character to mimic the reading, thinking and typing speed of humans(Jones and Bergen, 2024):

The Model Caller typically requires time to generate responses with LLMs. During this period, the Input Listener and Output Sender continuously work to maintain the dialogue history. Once a query is completed, if the user has sent new messages during this time, the Model Caller initiates the next query; otherwise, it waits for a time interval $\hat{t}$ before processing the accumulated dialogue history to generate new responses. If new messages are generated, any unsent messages from the previous batch are cleared to maintain the conversation flow.

# 3.3 Pseudo-Dialogue Generation

To enhance the efficiency of the Turing test, we propose to let the LLMs direct the progression of the test by synthesizing extended user-machine interaction through dialogue generation. Classical open-domain conversational data generation generally includes three steps: (1) Input generation: Provide fundamental information to initiate the conversation that specifies the topic and personalized style, i.e., conversation seed; (2) Utterance generation: Utilize the conversation seed to generate a multi-turn conversation; (3) Quality filtering: Eliminate samples that fail to meet the quality criteria (Soudani et al., 2024). The quality filtering step is omitted as our dialogue generation process aims to reflect the genuine evolving performance of the LLM over prolonged interaction.

Thus, we propose the $X$ -turn Pass Rate metric to evaluate the possibility that the model can pass the Turing test within specified turns of dialogue. To compute the metric over $N$ pairs of $X$ -turn dialogues, we ask $K$ judges (with $K = 1$ for each LLM judge) to differentiate between each pair, comprising a human-human and a human-machine conversation. We record the number of judges who accurately identify the human-machine conversation in each pair as $C = \{C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_N\}$ , where $C_i$ represents the count for the $i$ -th pair. The pass rate for the model in $X$ turns is then calculated by: $$ \mathrm {P a s s R a t e} = 1 - \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \left(\frac {C _ {i}}{K}\right) $$ This metric evaluates the proportion of dialogues in which the judges fail to distinguish between human and machine. A higher X-turn pass rate signifies more human-like performance by the LLM, indicating greater success in the test. # 4.3 Results Table 1 shows the pass rates under different dialogue settings and judges. The 110-turn Turing test is conducted with a sequence of 100-turn pseudodialogue generation followed by a 10-turn interaction between human and machine. The results highlight a significant influence of dialogue length on model performance. According to the human judges, GPT-4 maintains a consistently higher average pass rate across all tested turns compared with other models, achieving the best average 3-turn pass rate of $51.9\%$ . However, as the dialogue progresses, the average word count per message has significantly increased and both models generally exhibited a significant decrease in their pass rates, showcasing the necessity of long Turing tests. Gap Between Human and LLM Judgment As the number of testing turns increases, all judges become increasingly adept at distinguishing between LLM and human interlocutors, resulting in a decreasing pass rate with an increased number of turns. However, the disparity between human and AI evaluatio

Gap Between Human and LLM Judgment As the number of testing turns increases, all judges become increasingly adept at distinguishing between LLM and human interlocutors, resulting in a decreasing pass rate with an increased number of turns. However, the disparity between human and AI evaluation is evident. Human judges generally perceive GPT-4 and Claude-3-Sonnet as more human-like in conversations, whereas both LLMs tend to prefer Qwen-110B. Moreover, when presented with identical dialogues, human judges are generally more accurate in differentiating between LLM and human, contributing to a lower pass rate. This gap highlights the insufficiency of models in understanding and simulating real-world communications. Consequently, analysis in subsequent sections will primarily rely on assessments from human judges.

Comparison Between Dialogue Settings Comparing the extended burst dialogue setting with the classical ping-pong setting reveals notable differ

ences. Although characterized by more complex information exchanges, all models better mimic human messaging habits in the number of words per message under the burst setting. However, performance variations exist between the two patterns, with Claude-3-Sonnet and Qwen-110B excelling in burst dialogues, while GPT-4 performs better in ping-pong dialogues. Therefore, as a natural form of textual communication in human life, challenges presented by burst dialogue are also worthy of attention.

# 5 Discussion

In this section, we investigate other significant factors that have an impact on the X-TURING and ultimate evaluation results.

# 5.1 Dialogue History Quantity

A pivotal consideration of having LLM play a specific role in giving utterances is determining the necessary amount of utterances. To explore this, we analyze how the quantity of dialogue history provided for the model affects the pass rates of the Turing test, as presented in Table 2. Generally, providing more dialogue history enables models to better simulate human conversational styles, thereby increasing their pass rate. This effect is particularly pronounced in burst dialogue, where additional dialogue examples are markedly effective. However, the benefit of increasing the given dialogue diminishes once a certain threshold is surpassed. Moreover, the consistency of the dialogue style plays a crucial role. Redundant or low-quality data can lead to anomalies, such as GPT-4 performing better given 50 turns of ping-pong dialogue data compared to 100 turns. This highlights the importance of both the quantity and quality of dialogue history in effectively helping LLMs through the Turing Test.

# 5.3 Topic Analysis

Considering the varying amounts and qualities of data in the pretraining corpora for different topics, the capacity of models to generate contextually appropriate responses could be different. It is necessary to investigate the impact of topics on the

test while ensuring a comprehensive and balanced distribution. As shown in Figure 6, there is an evident disparity in how different models perform on distinct topics at shorter dialogue duration (3-turn and 10-turn). For instance, GPT-4 excels in Technology, while Claude-3-Sonnet shows a higher aptitude in School-related topics and Qwen-110B has a relative strength in Climate discussions. However, a common challenge among all three models is observed in the Art category, suggesting that the creative and interpretive nature of artistic discussions presents a difficulty for LLMs in achieving human-level conversation. However, as dialogue lengthens to 100 turns, the overall average performance declines and the ability to sustain consistent interaction becomes a more dominant factor, overshadowing the advantages or disadvantages that particular topics might offer.

The comparative analysis emphasizes GPT-4's enhanced ability to preserve human-like qualities over prolonged interactions compared to Qwen-110B, despite still failing to deceive humans effectively. This finding aligns with the human evaluation results presented in Table 1. # 6.2 Interaction Samples Figure 8 highlights the differences between AI and human responses at the first and 101st turn (after 100 pseudo-dialogue turns) in two distinct dialogue settings. In both dialogue types, the LLMs initially mirror human conversational tactics effectively, utilizing informal slang and abbreviations, and maintaining brevity. However, as the conversations progress to the 101st turn, notable discrepancies begin to appear. Notably, in the Ping-Pong dialogue format, Qwen begins to produce overly lengthy responses, a deviation from the concise exchanges typically observed in natural human interactions. This extended message length makes the conversation feel less natural and more mechanical, as reported by most of the judges. Moreover, while the use of emoticons by LLMs aims to enhance emotional expressiveness, it often misses the mark in its execution. Rather than expressing emotions with emoticons as how they are typically employed in human text conversations, responses by LLMs like Qwen-110B often feature an overuse of emojis that summarize the textual content. These issues underscore the ongoing challenges LLMs face in replicating the nuanced flow and emotional subtlety of human conversations. # 7 Conclusion In summary, our study introduces the X-TURING framework that effectively and efficiently evaluates the human likeness of LLMs through pseudodialogue generation with extended dialogue settings. With the definition of the X-Turn Pass-Rate metric, our experiments reveal that GPT-4 outperforms other tested models across most configurations and evaluation criteria, achieving an average $51.9\%$ and $38.9\%$ pass rate in 3-turn and 10-turn dialogue respectively. However, as dialogue length increases through iteratively generating dialogues that approximate human-machine interactions, the pass rates for all models significantly drop. Our analysis highlights the critical influence of dialogue duration and complexity on LLMs' performance in Turing tests and suggests directions for refining evaluation methods to enhance efficiency and reliability. # Limitations While our study presents an innovative approach to efficiently evaluating LLMs using the extended Turing test framework, the following limitations must be acknowledged: (1) Responses from LLMs are inherently influenced by user inputs and previous LLM-generated dialogue quality. Hence, using static evaluation techniques like questionnaires instead of real-time communication cannot eliminate the impact of the preferences of users participating in the conversation, which forms a trade-off between efficiency and accuracy. (2) Although we considered various participant factors such as age, educational background, and familiarity with AI, the subjective nature of human judgment in evaluating AI responses can lead to inconsistencies, which is an intrinsic characteristic of the Turing test. # Ethics Statement Our research involves collecting dialogue data and questionnaires from real human participants, and as such, we adhere to stringent ethical guidelines to ensure the privacy, consent, and well-being of all participants involved.
